The first passage emphasizes that the violence at Cawnpore was especially shocking because it was committed by a "subject race" against their "masters," including women and children, and describes it as a "servile war," a "war of race," and an act of rebellion by "black men" against white rulers. This framing presents the deaths as a racial betrayal, where those considered inferior dared to kill those considered superior.
